newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanians march again in port, Tirana rally banned.
newsitem.headline: Albanians march again in port, Tirana rally banned.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Albanians ruined by failed investment schemes thronged this port for the third day in a row on Friday and vowed to press on with daily rallies to oust the right-wing government.
The resumption of protests last month spread for the first time to the capital Tirana, where 1,000 demonstrators were dispersed by police, and to at least one other town.

But authorities banned a rally called by the newly-united opposition for Saturday in Tirana to denounce President Sali Berisha and emulate protests which won concessions from leaders in nearby Serbia and Bulgaria. Police cited security fears.
In Vlore, up to 30,000 people swarmed the streets in the early morning, joined by students pouring out of classrooms.
Demonstrators dispersed but returned in even greater numbers after dark, filling the square where Albania was proclaimed independent in 1912 after more than four centuries of Turkish rule.
"Every day to the square, every day in Vlore, every day in Tirana," shouted the marchers. "Tomorrow in Tirana," others replied in chorus.
Children carried torches made from cardboard boxes set alight and banners appeared for the first time, among them "Down with the corrupt government" and "We want no violence".
Opposition politicians travelling 150 km (90 mile) from the capital also made their first appearance alongside depositors.
"I've come here to breathe the free air of Vlore," said Neritan Ceka, President of the centre-right Democratic Alliance. "These people want change, not just their money."

Police gave up attempts to disperse protesters on the first day and were allowing them to move at will. Many officers, like all residents, had invested heavily in the local Gjallica firm which folded this week with $500 million owed to depositors.

In Tirana, state television said city police had withheld permission from the rally scheduled for Skanderbeg Square in the heart of the capital. It said defiance of the law would be met with "punishments as provided by the criminal code".
"We are calling for mass protests like in other Balkan countries," Socialist Party spokesman Kastriot Islami told Reuters Television.
Angry depositors who lost life savings set fire to public buildings in several Albanian cities late last month.
But more than 150 arrests and the threat of 15-year jail terms on public order charges had kept would-be protesters off the streets until the protests resumed in Vlore.
Eyewitnesses said up to 1,000 people had massed outside the Tirana home of Sude, a Gypsy woman whose pyramid scheme failed owing about $60 million to100,000 depositors.
Riot police arrived in force and dispersed the gathering. Sude is one of several pyramid scheme operators under arrest.

About 1,000 protesters in the town of Memaliaj blocked a bridge on the main road south to Greece, confronted by troops. Protesters said they trusted neither the government nor the opposition and wanted an "imported government".

Schemes offering quick, lucrative returns have flourished in post-Communist Albania. Protesters accuse Berisha of failing to warn of the pitfalls and some opposition politicians say the Democratic Party used their proceeds to win re-election last year in polls denounced as unfair by Western observers.
Economists say some $2 billion was invested altogether. Depositors are now receiving partial refunds of deposits from two failed firms but payouts are slow and chaotic.
Berisha has made no public appearances since chairing cross-party talks on Tuesday on easing the plight of investors.
